query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the atomic-scale lattice distortion in lightweight HEAs by incorporating a minor amount of a small-radius element (e.g., Mg) simultaneously strengthens the alloy via dislocation pinning and promotes the nucleation of a more uniform and adherent surface oxide/passivation film, thereby enhancing both mechanical performance and resistance to corrosion and high‐temperature oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline lightweight HEA (for example, an AlTiVNb alloy) exhibiting moderate lattice distortion and a single-phase microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, small addition of a light, small-radius element (such as Mg) to increase local atomic size mismatch and lattice distortion without significantly altering density.
generation.conditions: Perform room‐temperature tensile tests and electrochemical corrosion tests in a 0.6 M NaCl solution to assess mechanical strength and corrosion resistance, and conduct high‐temperature oxidation tests at around 700 °C to evaluate oxidation behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortion modifies local grain boundary energies and the electronic structure at near-surface regions, which mediates both dislocation pinning in the bulk and the nucleation/stability of oxide/passivation films at the surface.
generation.mechanism: The increased lattice distortion restricts dislocation motion, thereby raising yield strength, while simultaneously generating a higher density of favorable nucleation sites at grain boundaries and surfaces that support the formation of a uniform, adherent oxide layer. This oxide film improves corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline HEA, the Mg-enhanced alloy should exhibit (1) higher yield strength due to stronger dislocation pinning, (2) a more uniform and stable surface oxide layer (as observed by TEM/XPS) under both corrosive and high-temperature oxidative conditions, and (3) lower corrosion current densities in electrochemical tests.
generation.baseline: The baseline alloy is the unmodified lightweight HEA (e.g., AlTiVNb) with only its inherent lattice distortion.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis may cease to hold if the added Mg exceeds a threshold that induces phase separation, precipitation of brittle intermetallics, or if external conditions (such as extreme oxygen pressures or drastic thermal cycling) dominate the oxidation and corrosion kinetics regardless of the microstructural modifications.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal combines findings from PMC11330973 (demonstrating that nanoscale chemical fluctuations and induced lattice effects can significantly improve yield strength), and PMC9735962 (showing that amorphous or chemically homogeneous microstructures enhance corrosion resistance). The new aspect is the proposed direct mechanistic link between deliberately enhanced lattice distortion and the promotion of stable oxide/passivation film formation—a linkage not directly explored in prior studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: (a) the baseline lightweight HEA (e.g., AlTiVNb) and (b) a modified version with a minor, controlled addition of Mg to enhance lattice distortion. Subject both sample sets to identical processing conditions. Then perform room-temperature tensile tests, electrochemical corrosion testing in 0.6 M NaCl, and high-temperature oxidation exposure at ~700 °C. Characterize the microstructure, dislocation density (via TEM), oxide film uniformity (via XPS and SEM), and mechanical properties.
measurements: Yield strength and ductility from tensile testing
Corrosion current density from electrochemical impedance and polarization tests
Oxide layer uniformity, thickness, and adhesion from TEM/XPS analyses
Dislocation density and microstructural homogeneity from TEM analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mg-enhanced alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both mechanical strength (i.e., yield strength increase and maintained ductility) and a demonstrably more uniform/stable oxide film (resulting in lower corrosion current densities and improved high-temperature oxidation resistance) when compared to the baseline, then the proposed mechanistic link between lattice distortion and protective film formation will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: While making lightweight HEAs, it is common practice to incorporate significant amounts of light components such as aluminium, titanium, magnesium, and lithium. The incorporation of Al (also for the purpose of alloy strengthening) changes the phase composition and microstructure of HEAs to produce a multiphase microstructure that can include FCC, BCC, and B2 structures [,], and the incorporation of Ti can easily lead to the production of secondary phases. Single-phase equiatomic AlCrTiV HEA has a low density of 5.06 g/cm3 and a hardness of 498 HV. The AlCrTiV quaternary system was selected by Huang et al. [], who further increased the material’s hardness by including lightweight microalloying components. Microalloyed AlCrTiV alloys have a maximum hardness of 710 HV and a density of around 4.5 g per cubic centimeter. In addition to their mechanical advantages, high-performance additives provide excellent resistance to corrosion, which is an important factor in the application of engineering and structural materials.

On the other hand, to further verify the accuracy of the simulation results, as-cast HfxNbTaxTiZr HEA samples (x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) were prepared and tested to compare with the simulation results. The tensile stress–strain curve obtained from the test is shown in Figure 4e. The tensile yield strengths of HEAs with different compositions were calculated based on the simulation curves and compared with the tensile strengths obtained by testing. The comparison results are shown in Figure 4f. It can be seen from the comparison results that the variation trend of the simulated values is in line with the actual test results. The variation trend of dislocation density shown in Figure 5 also provides evidence.

AbstractDeveloping light yet strong aluminum (Al)-based alloys has been attracting unremitting efforts due to the soaring demand for energy-efficient structural materials. However, this endeavor is impeded by the limited solubility of other lighter components in Al. Here, we propose to surmount this challenge by converting multiple brittle phases into a ductile solid solution in Al-based complex concentrated alloys (CCA) by applying high pressure and temperature. We successfully develop a face-centered cubic single-phase Al-based CCA, Al55Mg35Li5Zn5, with a low density of 2.40 g/cm3 and a high specific yield strength of 344×103 N·m/kg (typically ~ 200×103 N·m/kg in conventional Al-based alloys). Our analysis reveals that formation of the single-phase CCA can be attributed to the decreased difference in atomic size and electronegativity between the solute elements and Al under high pressure, as well as the synergistic high entropy effect caused by high temperature and high pressure. The increase in strength originates mainly from high solid solution and nanoscale chemical fluctuations. However, the strong HEA films mentioned above suffer from low ductility in general. How to balance the strength and ductility of amorphous HEA films is important for their applications in the field of flexible microelectronic devices and mechanical metamaterials. In addition, seeking a high-performance HEA film with low density and corrosion resistance is of great significance for their applications in extreme conditions. In these cases, it is crucial to develop a high hardness, high strength–ductility synergy, and excellent corrosion resistance of amorphous lightweight high entropy alloy film. In this work, the lightweight AlTiVNb HEA film was prepared by magnetron sputtering, and the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance were investigated.
